psle.title: The Map That Refused to Stay Dry
psle.body:
During the school camp, Arun was chosen to lead his group along a marked forest trail. He had checked the map twice and liked the reassuring weight of the compass in his pocket. Halfway through the walk, a sudden shower swept across the trees. By the time the group reached a shelter, rain had blurred one corner of the map.

Arun wanted to continue before another team caught up. Mei noticed that the damaged section covered the next junction. She suggested comparing the visible landmarks with the emergency route card fixed inside the shelter. Arun hesitated. Stopping felt like falling behind, yet guessing would place everyone else inside his decision.

The group spent four minutes matching a stream, a footbridge and the direction of the slope. They discovered that the path Arun first chose would have led away from the campsite. When they finally arrived, they were not the first team back. However, the instructor praised the group for using evidence and checking a risky assumption. Arun folded the damp map carefully. For once, arriving later did not feel like losing.
psle.q: Why did arriving later not feel like losing to Arun?
opts: He learnt that the instructor always rewards the last team.
He realised that checking evidence and keeping the group safe mattered more than being the first team back.
He discovered that the other teams had used the wrong trail.
He was pleased because the damaged map no longer belonged to him.
psle.model: Arriving later did not feel like losing because Arun realised that checking the evidence and protecting his group from a risky guess were more important than returning first.
psle.evidence: The instructor praised the group for using evidence and checking a risky assumption.
marks: Meaning point: explains Arun's changed view of success.
Support point: links the delay to checking evidence and keeping the group safe.

news.title: Pupils Map Cooler Walking Routes
news.meta: Singapore news-style reading · 6-minute read · Original practice
news.body:
A group of Primary 5 pupils tested how shade changes the experience of walking near their school. They divided two routes into short sections and recorded the air temperature, surface temperature and amount of shade at the same times on three afternoons.

The pupils expected the shortest route to feel most comfortable. Their measurements showed a different pattern. A slightly longer path with mature trees had cooler ground surfaces and more continuous shade. The team also interviewed older residents, who explained that benches and safe road crossings affected which route they would actually use.

The pupils did not declare one route the winner. Instead, they created a map showing different needs: a faster route, a shadier route and a route with more resting points. Their teacher said the project demonstrated why a useful recommendation should combine measurements with the experiences of the people affected.
news.q: Why did the pupils create a map with several route choices instead of naming one winning route?
opts: They could not agree on any of their temperature readings.
They recognised that different walkers value speed, shade, resting points and safe crossings differently.
Their teacher did not allow them to compare routes.
They wanted residents to avoid every route near the school.
news.model: The pupils created several route choices because the best route depends on a walker's needs, such as speed, shade, places to rest and safe crossings.
news.evidence: The project combined measurements with the experiences of the people affected.
marks: Meaning point: identifies that different walkers have different needs.
Support point: names relevant route factors such as speed, shade, rests or crossings.

math.title: Logic Lab · Coral Gates
math.q: Four coral gates J, K, L and M form a row. K is immediately after J. L is after M. M is not first. Which order is possible?
opts: J, K, M, L
M, J, K, L
J, M, K, L
L, J, K, M
math.model: J, K, M, L is possible. K is immediately after J, L is after M, and M is not first.
steps: Underline the three conditions.
Reject an option as soon as one condition fails.
Check the surviving option against all three conditions again.
marks: Method mark: checks each option against all three conditions.
Answer mark: selects J, K, M, L.

science.title: Electrical Diagrams · Open Switch
science.q: A circuit has a working cell and bulb, but the switch is open. Which is the best complete explanation for why the bulb does not light?
opts: The open switch stores all the current.
The open switch creates a gap, making the circuit incomplete, so electric current cannot flow through the bulb.
The cell loses all its energy whenever a switch opens.
The bulb needs two switches before current can flow.
science.model: The open switch creates a gap, making the circuit incomplete. Therefore, electric current cannot flow through the bulb and it does not light.
steps: Locate the gap at the switch.
State that the circuit is incomplete.
Link the incomplete path to no current through the bulb.
marks: Science point: identifies the open switch as a gap that makes the circuit incomplete.
Evidence link: explains that current cannot flow through the bulb, so it does not light.

science.title: Heat Energy · Spoon Handles
science.q: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon are placed in hot soup. Why does the metal handle become warm sooner?
opts: Metal creates heat when it touches soup.
Metal is a better thermal conductor, so heat is transferred from the hotter soup to the cooler handle faster.
Wood sends coldness into the soup.
The metal spoon must have started at a higher temperature.
science.model: Metal is a better thermal conductor than wood, so heat is transferred from the hotter soup through the metal spoon to its cooler handle faster.
steps: Identify the hotter region: the soup.
State that heat moves from hotter to colder regions.
Compare the materials: metal conducts heat faster than wood.
marks: Science point: states that metal is a better thermal conductor than wood.
Evidence link: explains that heat reaches the cooler metal handle faster.

psle.title: The Pause Before the Launch
psle.meta: P5/P6 PSLE-style narrative · 7-minute read · Original practice
psle.body:
Evan's team had one final chance to launch its weather balloon before the judging window closed. The balloon was ready, the camera was recording, and the other teams had gathered beside the field. Just as the countdown began, Evan noticed that the wind sensor showed the same reading for the sixth time. The unmoving number looked suspicious, but everyone else was watching the clock.

He almost stayed silent. During earlier rehearsals, his teammates had teased him for checking every cable twice. Stopping now might make him seem afraid of failure. Then Evan remembered that the balloon would drift beyond the recovery zone if the wind estimate was wrong. He raised his hand and asked for the launch to be paused.

The team leader frowned but agreed to a quick test. A loose connector was keeping the sensor display frozen. By the time they repaired it, the judging window had closed. Their balloon never left the ground that afternoon. Evan expected the team to blame him. Instead, the leader placed the faulty connector beside their project log and said, 'This is part of our result too. We found evidence that our plan was not yet safe.'

On the journey home, Evan still wished they had launched. However, he no longer confused courage with rushing forward. Sometimes courage meant being the person who asked everyone to stop and look again.
psle.q: Why did Evan no longer see pausing the launch as a sign of weakness?
opts: He learnt that the judges always rewarded teams whose balloons remained on the ground.
He realised that raising an evidence-based concern protected the team from an unsafe decision, even though speaking up was difficult.
He wanted to delay the launch so that the other teams would finish first.
He believed that repairing one connector guaranteed that the team would win the next competition.
psle.model: Evan no longer saw the pause as weakness because he realised that speaking up about suspicious evidence prevented the team from making an unsafe decision, even though it was difficult to stop everyone.
psle.evidence: Sometimes courage meant being the person who asked everyone to stop and look again.
marks: Meaning point: explains Evan's new understanding of courage.
Support point: links his decision to the faulty reading and the risk of an unsafe launch.

news.title: Pupils Test Quieter Study Corners
news.meta: Singapore news-style reading · 6-minute read · Original practice
news.body:
Primary school pupils working with a community library have tested three movable panels designed to create quieter study corners. The panels used different arrangements of recycled felt, cardboard channels and ventilation gaps.

During each test, the pupils placed a speaker at the same distance from a sound meter and played the same recording at the same volume. Panel C reduced the measured sound level the most. At first, the team expected to recommend it immediately.

A second set of observations changed their view. Temperature readings rose more quickly behind Panel C because its thick layers left little space for air to move. Library users who tried the corner also said that it felt warm after ten minutes. Panel B reduced slightly less noise but allowed better airflow and received more comfortable ratings.

The pupils will repeat the trials at busier times before making a final recommendation. Their report will show the sound readings, temperature changes and user comments together. The librarian said that a useful design should solve the original problem without creating a new one.
news.q: Why did the pupils decide not to recommend Panel C immediately?
opts: Panel C produced no change in the measured sound level.
They found that Panel C reduced noise well but also trapped warmer air, so they needed to consider both quietness and user comfort.
The library users refused to enter any study corner containing recycled material.
They wanted to choose the panel with the highest temperature reading.
news.model: The pupils did not recommend Panel C immediately because, although it reduced noise the most, it also allowed less airflow and became warmer, so the team had to consider comfort as well as sound reduction.
news.evidence: Panel C reduced the measured sound level the most, but temperature readings rose more quickly behind it and users said that it felt warm.
marks: Meaning point: identifies the trade-off instead of judging the design by one measurement.
Support point: compares Panel C's stronger noise reduction with its poorer airflow or comfort.

math.title: Angles · Signal Rays
math.tag: Connect vertically opposite angles and split an angle
math.q: Straight lines P-O-R and Q-O-S intersect at O. Ray OT lies inside angle ROS. Angle POQ is 128° and angle ROT is 37°. Find angle TOS. The diagram is not drawn to scale.
math.visual: <svg viewBox='0 0 420 245' role='img' aria-label='Two straight lines intersect at O and ray OT divides angle ROS'><line x1='45' y1='115' x2='375' y2='115' stroke='#1557c0' stroke-width='6' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='292' y1='15' x2='128' y2='215' stroke='#1557c0' stroke-width='6' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='210' y1='115' x2='327' y2='203' stroke='#0a8a63' stroke-width='6' stroke-linecap='round'/><circle cx='210' cy='115' r='9' fill='#ff7b6b'/><g fill='#073b86' font-size='18' font-weight='800'><text x='24' y='108'>P</text><text x='382' y='108'>R</text><text x='296' y='18'>Q</text><text x='110' y='231'>S</text><text x='334' y='218'>T</text><text x='194' y='105'>O</text><text x='145' y='58'>128°</text><text x='281' y='145'>37°</text><text x='218' y='195'>x°</text></g></svg>
math.model: Angle ROS = angle POQ = 128° because vertically opposite angles are equal. Therefore, angle TOS = 128° - 37° = 91°.
steps: Use the intersecting straight lines: angle ROS is vertically opposite angle POQ, so angle ROS = 128°.
Ray OT splits angle ROS into angle ROT and angle TOS.
Subtract the known part: angle TOS = 128° - 37° = 91°.
marks: Method mark: identifies angle ROS as 128° using vertically opposite angles.
Answer mark: subtracts 37° and gives angle TOS = 91°.

science.title: Water Cycle · Two Rain Chambers
science.q: Two sealed rain chambers contain equal amounts of warm water. Chamber A has an 8°C metal lid and produces 18 drops from its lid in five minutes. Chamber B has a 25°C metal lid and produces 3 drops in the same time. Which is the best complete explanation for the difference?
opts: The cold lid in Chamber A creates new water and pushes it through the metal.
Only Chamber A contains water vapour because evaporation cannot occur under a warmer lid.

Water evaporates in both chambers. In Chamber A, the water vapour loses heat faster at the cooler lid and condenses into liquid droplets more quickly, so more droplets combine and fall in five minutes.
The warm water in Chamber B freezes before it can reach the lid.
science.visual:
🧊Chamber A8°C lid
18 drops
↔
🌡️Same warm waterequal amount
same five minutes
↔
💧Chamber B25°C lid
3 drops
science.model: Water evaporates in both sealed chambers. In Chamber A, water vapour loses heat faster when it reaches the cooler 8°C lid, so it condenses into liquid water droplets more quickly. More droplets therefore combine and fall from the lid within five minutes.
steps: Compare only the changed condition: the lid temperature is lower in Chamber A, while the amount of warm water and time are the same.
Trace the process: liquid water evaporates, and the water vapour reaches each lid.
Link evidence to result: faster heat loss at the cooler lid causes faster condensation, matching the larger number of drops in Chamber A.
marks: Science point: states that water vapour loses heat at the cooler lid and condenses into liquid droplets.
Evidence link: uses the controlled comparison and 18-versus-3 drop result to explain the faster condensation in Chamber A.

scienceVocab.meaning: water in its gaseous state cannot be seen, although it can be present in the surrounding air
scienceVocab.example: The invisible water vapour later formed visible droplets on the cooler lid.
scienceVocab.note: OEQ warning: clouds and mist are tiny water droplets, not visible water vapour.

scienceVocab.term: loses heat at a cooler surface
scienceVocab.meaning: transfers heat to a surface at a lower temperature
scienceVocab.example: The water vapour loses heat when it reaches the cooler metal lid.
scienceVocab.note: Name both the substance and the cooler surface instead of writing only 'it became cold'.

scienceVocab.meaning: changes from water vapour to small drops of liquid water after losing heat
scienceVocab.example: After losing heat, the water vapour condenses into liquid water droplets on the lid.
scienceVocab.note: High-scoring sequence: water vapour loses heat -> condenses -> liquid droplets form.

scienceVocab.meaning: small liquid droplets join to form larger drops that are pulled down by gravity
scienceVocab.example: The droplets combine and fall from the sloping lid like rain.
scienceVocab.note: Use this phrase only after explaining how the droplets formed.

scienceVocab.meaning: a result that can be linked to one changed condition because other relevant conditions were kept the same
scienceVocab.example: The 18-versus-3 drop result is evidence from a controlled comparison of lid temperature.
scienceVocab.note: OEQ use: name what changed, what stayed the same and the measured result.

chinese.title: P5 华文短文阅读 · 看见别人的贡献
chinese.q: 班级要参加节水宣传比赛。文浩画图很快，说话也很有信心，因此总觉得动作较慢的宇杰帮不上忙。宇杰没有争辩，只是把大家讨论过的资料整理好，还用硬纸板做了一个不用电的展示架。比赛当天，活动室突然停电，原本准备好的电子画面无法播放。正当大家手忙脚乱时，宇杰拿出展示架，把整理好的图表一张张放上去。小组顺利完成介绍，还得到评审的称赞。活动结束后，文浩重新制作名单，并把宇杰的名字写在最前面。
chinese.ask: 文浩为什么把宇杰的名字写在最前面？
opts: 因为宇杰要求文浩把自己列为组长。
因为文浩认识到宇杰虽然做事较慢，却准备得认真周到，并在停电时帮助小组顺利完成介绍。
因为文浩不再愿意参加节水宣传比赛。
因为评审只称赞了宇杰制作的展示架。
chinese.model: 文浩把宇杰的名字写在最前面，是因为他终于看见宇杰认真周到的准备。停电时，宇杰制作的展示架和整理好的图表帮助小组顺利完成介绍，使文浩明白贡献不能只用做事速度来判断。
marks: 内容点：说明文浩改变了对宇杰的看法。
依据点：写出宇杰事先认真准备，并在停电时帮助小组完成介绍。

psle.title: The List Beside the Door
psle.meta: P5/P6 PSLE-style narrative · 7-minute read · Original practice
psle.body:
On the morning of the school innovation showcase, Soren checked his team's display three times. The model bridge stood neatly on the table, and every label was in place. When his teammate Hana suggested testing the bridge once more with the heaviest weight, Soren shook his head. The judges would arrive soon, and he did not want to disturb a display that already looked perfect.

Hana pointed to a small list taped beside the door. It was the team's test checklist: check the joints, add weights one at a time, and record what changes. Soren remembered that they had only tested the bridge with light wooden blocks. Reluctantly, he agreed. At the third heavier block, one joint bent downwards.

The team had only minutes left, but they used two short supports to strengthen that joint. During the showcase, the bridge held the full set of weights. Afterwards, Soren did not praise Hana for making the display look better. He thanked her for noticing that a neat-looking model was not the same as tested evidence.
psle.q: Why did Soren change his mind about testing the bridge again?
opts: He wanted to make the bridge look less neat before the judges arrived.
He realised that the bridge had not been tested with the heaviest weights, so its appearance was not enough evidence that it would work safely.
He believed that heavy wooden blocks always damage any bridge.
He wanted Hana to complete the whole showcase alone.
psle.model: Soren changed his mind because the checklist reminded him that the bridge had only been tested with light blocks. He realised that a neat appearance was not evidence that it could safely hold the heaviest weight.
psle.evidence: They had only tested the bridge with light wooden blocks.
marks: Meaning point: states that Soren needed evidence from a heavier-weight test.
Support point: links the decision to the earlier test using only light blocks.

news.title: Pupils Help Plan a Safer Cycling Route
news.meta: Singapore news-style reading · 6-minute read · Original practice
news.body:
Pupils from a neighbourhood school have worked with residents to study a short cycling route near a community centre. The route is popular after school, but several adults said that younger riders sometimes turn quickly around a blind corner.

The pupils first counted riders at the same half-hour on five weekdays. They also drew where riders slowed down, rang their bells or stopped. The highest number of sudden stops happened near a hedge that blocked the view of people walking from the opposite direction.

Instead of asking only for a new sign, the pupils proposed trimming part of the hedge, painting a slower-speed marking before the corner and adding a small mirror. A town council representative said the group had made a useful recommendation because it connected observations with more than one possible safety measure.
news.q: Why did the pupils propose several safety measures instead of only a new sign?
opts: They wanted to make the cycling route longer for every rider.
Their observations showed that the blind corner involved both poor visibility and sudden stopping, so they suggested measures that addressed more than one part of the problem.
They did not collect any information about the route.
The town council asked them to remove all bicycles from the neighbourhood.
news.model: The pupils suggested several measures because their observations showed more than one safety issue: the hedge reduced visibility and riders often stopped suddenly. Trimming, road markings and a mirror address different parts of that problem.
news.evidence: The highest number of sudden stops happened near a hedge that blocked the view.
marks: Meaning point: identifies the linked visibility and stopping problem.
Support point: connects the observations to the range of suggested measures.

math.title: Percentage · Club Donation Goal
math.tag: Compare a completed percentage with the whole
math.q: A school club has collected $168, which is 70% of its donation goal. After a parent adds $36, what percentage of the goal has the club collected?
math.model: If 70% is $168, then 10% is $24 and 100% is $240. After the extra $36, the club has $204. $204 is 85% of $240.
steps: Find the whole goal: $24 × 10 = $240.
marks: Method mark: finds the whole donation goal correctly.
Answer mark: states that $204 is 85% of $240.

science.title: Plant Reproduction · Pollinator Access
science.q: Three similar flowers were kept in the same garden. Flower A was covered with a fine mesh bag before it opened. Flower B was left uncovered. Flower C was covered only after insects had visited it. Later, A produced no fruit, while B and C produced fruit. Which is the best complete explanation?
opts: The bag made Flower A too cold to grow leaves.
The bag prevented insects from transferring pollen to Flower A's stigma before it opened. Without pollination, fertilisation did not occur, so fruit did not form.
Flower B and C produced fruit because insects create seeds inside their bodies.
Flower A produced no fruit because all flowers need to be covered after insects visit.
science.model: The mesh bag prevented insects from transferring pollen grains to Flower A's stigma before it opened. Without pollination, fertilisation could not occur, so the ovary did not develop into a fruit.
steps: Compare when each flower was covered: only Flower A was blocked before insects could visit.
Insects transfer pollen from anthers to stigmas during pollination.
Without pollination and fertilisation, fruit and seeds cannot form.
marks: Science point: uses pollination and fertilisation in the correct sequence.
Evidence link: connects the early mesh bag on A to its lack of fruit.

scienceVocab.term: pollen grains are transferred to the stigma
scienceVocab.meaning: the pollination step in which pollen from an anther reaches a stigma of a flower of the same species
scienceVocab.example: An insect transfers pollen grains to the stigma when it visits another similar flower.
scienceVocab.note: OEQ order: pollen transfer happens before fertilisation.

scienceVocab.meaning: pollen cannot reach the stigma because an agent such as an insect is blocked
scienceVocab.example: The mesh bag prevents pollination by blocking insects from the flower.
scienceVocab.note: State what is blocked and why it matters.

scienceVocab.meaning: the male and female reproductive cells do not fuse after pollen fails to reach the stigma
scienceVocab.example: Without pollination, fertilisation does not occur in the flower.
scienceVocab.note: Do not use pollination and fertilisation as if they mean the same thing.

scienceVocab.term: the ovary develops into a fruit
scienceVocab.meaning: after fertilisation, the ovary grows to form the fruit
scienceVocab.example: After fertilisation, the ovary develops into a fruit containing seeds.
scienceVocab.note: Useful paired fact: ovules develop into seeds.

scienceVocab.term: evidence from the timing of a comparison
scienceVocab.meaning: a conclusion supported by noticing when a changed condition happened relative to the result
scienceVocab.example: Only the flower covered before insect visits produced no fruit, which is evidence that pollinator access mattered.
scienceVocab.note: OEQ pattern: name the different timing, then link it to the different result.

chinese.title: P5 华文短文阅读 · 从提醒到承担
chinese.q: 班级负责布置阅读角。开始时，俊豪只挑自己喜欢的海报设计，还嫌小敏一直核对书架编号太慢。活动前一天，老师发现有一箱新书没有分类。小敏拿出早已写好的编号表，带着大家一格一格放好。俊豪这才发现，如果没有小敏的细心，明天同学们根本找不到想看的书。活动结束后，他主动留下来，把自己设计的海报贴在正确的书架旁。
chinese.ask: 俊豪后来主动留下来贴海报，主要说明了什么？
opts: 他只想让大家看见自己的海报设计。
他认识到细心分类的重要，也愿意承担责任，让阅读角真正方便同学使用。
他认为小敏做事太慢，所以决定不再和她合作。
他不喜欢阅读角里的新书。
chinese.model: 俊豪认识到小敏细心分类的重要，也明白阅读角要方便同学使用，不能只追求海报好看。因此他主动留下来，把海报贴在正确的书架旁，愿意承担责任。
marks: 内容点：写出俊豪认识到分类和责任的重要。
依据点：结合小敏的编号表和俊豪贴海报的行为说明。

psle.title: The Question on the Clipboard
psle.meta: P5/P6 PSLE-style narrative · 7-minute read · Original practice
psle.body:
Leo had spent two weekends building a small automatic plant-watering device for the school fair. When it finally poured water into the pot, he took a short video and began preparing his display board. His sister watched the video twice, then asked why the device had watered the plant after only a few drops of rain.

Leo replied that the sensor had worked exactly as planned. Still, he wrote her question on a clipboard. The next afternoon, he placed the device outside while using a measuring cup to add small, equal amounts of water to the sensor tray. He discovered that water collected at one corner and touched both metal contacts earlier than he expected.

Leo raised the tray slightly and tested it again. This time, the pump started only after the amount of water he had chosen. At the fair, several visitors praised the device. Leo kept the first video too. It reminded him that a working result was not the end of an investigation; a good question could reveal what still needed checking.
psle.q: Why did Leo keep the first video after improving the device?
opts: He wanted to show that the first design was already perfect.
He wanted proof that visitors had praised him before the fair.
It reminded him that a result which seems to work can still need careful testing after a useful question is asked.
He planned to stop testing the device after recording the video.
psle.model: Leo kept the first video because it reminded him that the device appeared to work at first, but a useful question led him to test it more carefully and discover a problem with the water collecting too early.
psle.evidence: A working result was not the end of an investigation; a good question could reveal what still needed checking.
marks: Meaning point: explains that Leo valued further testing, not just the first working result.
Support point: links the question to discovering water reached the contacts too early.

news.title: Student Garden Team Tracks Food-Waste Compost
news.meta: Singapore news-style reading · 6-minute read · Original practice
news.body:
A school garden team has begun turning fruit peels and vegetable scraps from the canteen into compost. The pupils set up two covered compost boxes of the same size. Both boxes received equal amounts of food waste and dry leaves, but one box was mixed every three days while the other was left undisturbed.

For six weeks, the pupils recorded the temperature and appearance of the materials. The mixed box became darker and crumbly sooner. However, the group did not immediately claim that mixing was the only reason. They checked their records and noticed that both boxes had been kept in the same shaded area and had received the same amount of water.

The pupils will next test whether the compost helps bean plants grow. Their teacher said the project was strong because the team separated what they observed from what they could reasonably conclude.
news.q: Why did the pupils check that both compost boxes had the same location and amount of water?
opts: To make the comparison fairer, so the different mixing routine could be linked more confidently to the different results.
To ensure that neither compost box would change during the six weeks.
To prove that water is more important than food waste in every garden.
To make the undisturbed box receive more dry leaves.
news.model: The pupils kept the location and amount of water the same to make a fair comparison. This meant that the different mixing routine was the main changed condition they could link to the compost results.
news.evidence: Both boxes had been kept in the same shaded area and had received the same amount of water.
marks: Meaning point: identifies a fair comparison or controlled variables.
Support point: links the controlled conditions to testing the effect of mixing.

math.title: Fractions · Reef Badge Box
math.tag: Use the remaining fraction to rebuild the whole
math.q: Johnson has used 3/8 of the badges in a box. There are 30 badges left. How many badges were in the box at first?
math.model: If 3/8 has been used, 5/8 remains. Therefore, 5/8 is 30 badges. One eighth is 30 ÷ 5 = 6 badges, so the whole box has 8 × 6 = 48 badges.
steps: Find the remaining fraction: 1 − 3/8 = 5/8.
Use 5 equal parts = 30 to find one part: 30 ÷ 5 = 6.
Find all eight parts: 8 × 6 = 48.
marks: Method mark: recognises that 30 represents 5/8, not 3/8.
Answer mark: finds the original total of 48 badges.

science.focus: trace a substance through linked body systems
science.title: Human Systems · Fuel for a Race
science.q: Before a race, Mina eats a banana and drinks water. During the race, her leg muscles need energy. Which is the best complete explanation of how the banana helps the muscles?
opts: The banana stays in Mina's stomach and directly pushes her leg muscles faster.

The digestive system breaks the banana into small soluble nutrients. These are absorbed into the blood in the small intestine, and the circulatory system transports them to the leg muscles for respiration.
The lungs change the banana into oxygen before it reaches the muscles.
The heart digests the banana and stores all nutrients outside the body.
science.model: The digestive system breaks the banana into small soluble nutrients. The nutrients are absorbed through the small intestine into the blood. The circulatory system then transports them to Mina's leg muscles, where they are used in respiration to release energy.
steps: Food is digested into small soluble nutrients.
Nutrients are absorbed from the small intestine into the blood.
Blood transports nutrients to muscle cells, where respiration releases energy.
marks: Science point: states digestion, absorption and transport in the correct order.
Evidence link: connects the nutrients from the banana to energy release in working leg muscles.

scienceVocab.meaning: food substances made small enough by digestion to pass through the wall of the small intestine
scienceVocab.example: Digestion changes food into small soluble nutrients that can be absorbed.
scienceVocab.note: Do not write only 'small food'; use the word soluble.

scienceVocab.meaning: small soluble nutrients pass through the wall of the small intestine into blood vessels
scienceVocab.example: The digested nutrients are absorbed into the blood through the small intestine.

scienceVocab.meaning: blood carries useful substances such as oxygen and nutrients to cells around the body
scienceVocab.example: The circulatory system transports nutrients to the working muscle cells.
scienceVocab.note: Name what is carried and where it is carried to.

scienceVocab.term: used in respiration to release energy
scienceVocab.meaning: cells use nutrients and oxygen in respiration, releasing energy for activities
scienceVocab.example: Muscle cells use nutrients and oxygen in respiration to release energy for running.

scienceVocab.meaning: an explanation that traces a substance through more than one body system in sequence
scienceVocab.example: Food is digested, nutrients are absorbed into blood, and blood transports them to body cells.
scienceVocab.note: For 2 marks, keep the pathway in order and name the systems involved.

chinese.title: P5 华文短文阅读 · 先听再判断
chinese.q: 班会要选出环保活动的负责人。大家都推荐说话响亮的凯翔，小恩却一直没有举手。凯翔以为小恩不愿意帮忙，便在讨论时不耐烦地说：‘你有意见就快点说。’小恩拿出一张记录表，原来他这几天已经问过同学们最想参加什么活动，还把大家的想法分成了节水、回收和校园清洁三类。凯翔看完后安静下来，建议大家先用小恩的记录表安排任务。
chinese.ask: 凯翔后来建议使用小恩的记录表，说明他有了什么改变？
opts: 他认识到不能只凭一个人的表现判断别人，也开始重视小恩认真收集的意见。
他决定以后不参加任何环保活动。
他认为说话响亮的人不需要准备资料。
他想把所有同学的意见都删掉。
chinese.model: 凯翔原先只凭小恩没有举手就以为他不愿意帮忙。看了记录表后，他发现小恩已经认真收集和整理同学的意见，因此开始重视别人的实际贡献，不再轻易判断。
marks: 内容点：写出凯翔不再轻易判断别人，并重视实际贡献。
依据点：结合小恩收集、分类意见和凯翔采用记录表说明。
